title: KNAW Early Career Awards for research into piracy, quantum computing and politeness
excerpt: Twelve young researchers receive a KNAW Early Career Award, intended for up-and-coming young researchers who have innovative ideas for research or for such fields as education or patient care.
content:
21 October 2026

  • KNAW Early Career Award

Twelve young researchers receive a KNAW Early Career Award, intended for up-and-coming young researchers who have innovative ideas for research or for such fields as education or patient care. 

Up to twelve prizes are awarded annually, with each winner receiving a work of art and the sum of 15,000 euros, which they can invest in their own research career.
This year, the submission topics ranged from the maritime history of piracy to quantum computing, and from chemical process engineering to politeness in online political discourse.

Behavioural Sciences, Social Sciences and Law

Ivy Defoe 
Assistant professor, Child Development and Education, University of Amsterdam

Ivy Defoe studies high-risk behaviour in adolescents, contributing to a better understanding of how it develops. To further this research, she proposes to let teenagers themselves explain their own behaviour. 

In an article in the journal Nature, she advises scientists to study this phenomenon, which she refers to as ‘teensplaining’. In view of her work as a first-generation academic and her social engagement, the jury regards Defoe as a role model for a new generation of researchers.

Janske van Eersel
Postdoctoral researcher, Work and Organisational Psychology, Tilburg University

Losing a job can be a real blow. Janske van Eersel investigates grief associated with imminent or actual job loss. She studies how such grief arises, which factors cause people to experience complex grief, and what impact this has on their mental health and reintegration into the workforce. 

In addition, she combines her theoretical knowledge with practical applications, including assessment tools for professionals who counsel those facing a job loss or long-term sick leave. Her research has led to the emergence of a largely new field of study.

photo: Claudia Rison

Maša Galič
Assistant professor, Privacy and Criminal Law, VU Amsterdam

Maša Galič examines what digitalisation and the use of data in criminal investigations mean for criminal proceedings and the protection of fundamental rights. Her research concerns not only the trade-off between criminal investigations, privacy and the rights of suspects when processing bulk data, but also how to use technology effectively to protect fundamental rights.

Galič’s research and social engagement is helping to safeguard civil rights in an increasingly digital society.

Humanities

Erik de Lange

Assistant professor, Maritime Issues in International and Imperial History, Utrecht University

Erik de Lange studies the history of international relations at sea. He examines why it was precisely there that international rules and conflicts arose. He has shown how the battle against piracy in the Mediterranean led to European colonialism in North Africa. 

His popular history book on this topic was shortlisted for the Libris History Prize.
He is currently researching the sabotage and protection of submarine telegraph cables before and during World War I, highlighting what the past can teach us about current international tensions at sea and below the waves.

photo: Jeannette Huisman

Naomi Truan 
Assistant professor, German Sociolinguistics, Leiden University

Naomi Truan studies how polyglots use different languages, both online and offline as well as across national borders. Among other things, she examines language use in online communities and the role of issues like politeness in online discourse.

She also investigates how multilingual groups – for example Turkish-German women in Berlin and Moroccan-Dutch inhabitants of Rotterdam – use language and what their views are on the subject. She has recently turned her attention to the impact of AI on language use.

photo: Cherie Birkner

Laura De Vos 
Assistant professor, North American Studies and Indigenous Studies, Radboud University

What can we learn from Indigenous peoples when it comes to contemporary debates on colonialism, social justice and environmental responsibility? Assistant professor Laura De Vos studies the impact of Indigenous peoples in North America on political and cultural debate.

The jury describes their approach as interesting and refreshing in highlighting international solidarity with Indigenous activism. 

Medical, Biomedical and Health Sciences

Bahareh Goodarzi
Midwife, post-doctoral researcher and assistant professor, Reproductive Justice, University of Amsterdam and Amsterdam University Medical Center

Pregnant persons or babies from a non-Western migrant background consistently face a higher risk of illness, death and unnecessary medical interventions than their native Dutch counterparts. Bahareh Goodarzi wants to change that. Her research focuses on discrimination, equal rights and justice in maternity and neonatal care. 

The jury believes Goodarzi’s research is of immense social significance. Her popular science publications, podcasts and television appearances ensure that her research findings reach a wide audience.

photo: Luciano Ölz

Diego Pereira-Martins 
Research Associate, Haematology and Leukaemia, University Medical Center Groningen

Haematologist Diego Pereira-Martins conducts research into leukaemia, a collective name for various types of cancer affecting the body’s blood cells. In patients with leukaemia, genetic mutations cause pathogenic abnormalities in the body’s production of blood cells.

Pereira-Martins seeks to establish exactly how this works, and in doing so to uncover the mechanisms involved in leukaemia. His work serves as a baseline for a new clinical drug trial.

Anna Seijmonsbergen-Schermers
Midwife and assistant professor, Midwifery Science, Amsterdam University Medical Center

Anna Seijmonsbergen-Schermers studies how to provide the best possible support during childbirth. She also works as a self-employed midwife. Her research focuses on improving maternity care by taking a number of factors into account, including short-term outcomes and costs, women’s experiences, environmental impact, staffing levels and long-term outcomes. 

In addition, she presents research data in diagrams on her website, the aim being to clarify the real-world implications of the data and thereby empower pregnant persons to make choices that suit them.

photo: Gerhard Taatgen

Natural Sciences and Technology

Francesca Rizzo
Assistant professor, Astrophysics, University of Groningen

Galaxies can assume beautiful shapes; just consider spiral galaxies like our own Milky Way, with their curved, pinwheeling arms. But how do such shapes come into being over the course of millions and billions of years?

And what role does the mysterious, invisible dark matter play in all this? Astrophysicist Francesca Rizzo combines telescope images with new software to investigate these questions, and with great success.

Artur Schweidtmann
Assistant professor, Chemical Engineering, Delft University of Technology

Chemical process engineering is essential for the production of chemicals, fuels and materials used in a wide range of sectors. Chemical engineer Artur Schweidtmann combines machine learning with principles of physics to design chemical processes more intelligently and to make them run more efficiently and sustainably.

He has been highly successful at this, with his innovative research yielding methods that engineers can apply in real-world situations, ranging from process design to operational management.

John van de Wetering 
Assistant professor, Quantum Computing, University of Amsterdam

Quantum computing involves a special type of computer that uses quantum mechanics to perform sophisticated calculations extremely rapidly and efficiently, for example to simulate materials or molecules. A great deal of effort is going into developing the physical technology behind quantum computing.

John van de Wetering is studying methods to write quantum computing software that is both efficient and intuitive in its use. His innovations are already in widespread use in the field.
